paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every morning, millions of people reach for their phones before they are fully awake. Most could not explain why. Psychologists estimate that around forty per cent of our daily actions are not conscious decisions but habits: behaviours repeated so often that they happen automatically. Understanding how habits work has become a major area of research, and it offers practical lessons for anyone who wants to change their behaviour.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A habit has three parts, according to the researcher Charles Duhigg. First comes a cue, a trigger that tells the brain to start a routine. The routine is the behaviour itself, and the reward is the benefit that tells the brain the loop is worth remembering. For example, feeling stressed may lead to eating chocolate because it brings momentary comfort. Over time, the loop becomes so automatic that the brain barely needs to think.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This explains why willpower alone often fails. Trying to stop a habit without changing the cue and reward is like trying to push water uphill. Studies of people trying to give up smoking suggest that those who replaced the routine with another, such as chewing gum or taking a short walk, were more successful than those who simply tried to resist. The cue and the reward remained, but a new behaviour filled the gap.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How long does it take to form a new habit? A popular claim says twenty-one days, but this figure has little scientific basis. A study at University College London found that the average was sixty-six days, though individuals varied from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four. Simple habits, like drinking a glass of water after breakfast, formed faster than complex ones, such as exercising for half an hour. Missing a single day did not significantly damage progress, which should reassure anyone who worries about perfection.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Experts offer several suggestions for building good habits. Start small: a new routine that takes two minutes is easier to maintain than an ambitious one. Attach the new behaviour to an existing one, so that the old habit acts as a cue. And make the desired action easy, for instance by putting running shoes next to the bed. None of this is magic, but it works with the way the brain is built, rather than against it.
